title: NURS 1017 Unit 4 Case Study 1
description: 46-year-old female presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding from a benign, encapsulated uterine leiomyoma compared against a rapidly enlarging, fixed breast mass diagnosed as invasive ductal carcinoma requiring sentinel node biopsy.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the clinical intake and physical examination findings for Eleanor. Which assessment cues should the nurse recognize as highly characteristic of a malignant neoplasm rather than a benign tumor? Select all that apply.

options.text: Right breast mass that is hard, fixed to underlying pectoralis fascia, and exhibits irregular, poorly demarcated borders
Overlying cutaneous peau d'orange appearance with nipple retraction in the right breast
Palpable, firm, non-tender right axillary lymphadenopathy matted to surrounding soft tissue
Smooth, well-circumscribed, mobile, non-tender pelvic mass confirmed to be confined within a fibrous capsule
Gradual growth of a uterine myometrial mass over 6 years without regional tissue invasion
Unintended weight loss of 6 kg (13.2 lb) over the past 8 weeks accompanied by deep bone ache

question.explanation: Malignant neoplasms characteristically exhibit poorly demarcated, irregular borders, rapid infiltrative growth invading surrounding structural tissue (fixation to chest wall/pectoralis fascia), lymphatic invasion causing lymphedema/peau d'orange, and regional lymph node metastasis (firm, fixed axillary nodes). Systemic symptoms like significant unintentional weight loss and deep bone pain reflect advanced malignant progression and potential bony metastasis. Conversely, smooth, well-circumscribed, mobile, encapsulated masses that grow slowly over years without local invasion are classic hallmarks of benign neoplasms (such as a uterine leiomyoma).

leftContent.intro: The nurse in a comprehensive women's health and oncology center is conducting an intake assessment for Eleanor Vance, a 46-year-old female presenting for evaluation of two distinct lesions: a long-standing uterine mass and a newly discovered right breast lump.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 0830:Eleanor Vance, a 46-year-old female (G2P2), presents for evaluation. Gynecological history: has had a known uterine mass for 6 years, monitored by serial ultrasound, which produces menorrhagia (heavy menses) and mild lower abdominal pressure. Pelvic ultrasound from last week shows a 5.2 cm well-circumscribed, smoothly encapsulated intramural uterine leiomyoma with no abnormal vascularity or pelvic lymphadenopathy. Over the past 10 weeks, however, the client discovered a distinct, rapidly enlarging lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On inspection, there is subtle right nipple retraction and slight erythema with a 'peau d'orange' pitted skin texture over the right upper breast. On palpation, the breast mass is approximately 3.5 cm in diameter, stony hard, irregular, and immobile (fixed to underlying chest wall). Palpation of the right axilla reveals two enlarged, firm, non-tender lymph nodes measuring ~1.5 cm that feel matted together. Left breast and axilla are normal. Client reports feeling fatigued and notes an unintentional weight loss of 6 kg over the past 2 months. Vital signs stable. Nurse prepares client for diagnostic imaging and biopsy.

question.stem: The nurse analyzes the histopathological and clinical differences between the client's uterine mass and breast tumor. For each feature, click to specify whether it corresponds to a Benign Neoplasm (Leiomyoma) or a Malignant Neoplasm (Invasive Carcinoma).

rows.text: Encapsulated, well-differentiated smooth muscle cells resembling normal tissue of origin with low mitotic rate
Anaplastic, pleomorphic epithelial cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and abnormal mitoses
Infiltrative local tissue destruction with ability to invade lymphatic vessels and metastasize to distant organs
Slow, expansive growth that compresses surrounding tissue without penetrating adjacent tissue planes or basement membranes
High metabolic demand with central tumor ischemia, extensive necrosis, and induction of new vascular networks (tumor angiogenesis)
Typically designated by the suffix '-oma' added to parent cell type (e.g., adenoma, fibroma, chondroma)

question.preamble: Core needle biopsy results from the breast mass and pelvic imaging have been added to the client's electronic health record. The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1130 and the Diagnostic & Pathology Reports.
question.explanation:
1. Benign neoplasms: composed of well-differentiated cells that closely resemble the parent tissue, surrounded by a distinct fibrous capsule, slow expansive growth, absence of invasive or metastatic capabilities, and designated with suffix '-oma' (e.g., leiomyoma, adenoma).
2. Malignant neoplasms: characterized by anaplasia (loss of differentiation), cellular pleomorphism (variation in size and shape), hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei, infiltrative destruction of surrounding normal tissues, lack of encapsulation, rapid growth with central hemorrhage/necrosis, initiation of tumor angiogenesis, and the ability to invade lymphatics/blood vessels to establish distant metastases. Malignant epithelial tumors are termed 'carcinomas', while mesenchymal tumors are 'sarcomas'.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1300 and the Surgical Consult Plan.
question.explanation: Carcinomas arise from epithelial tissue; an adenocarcinoma specifically arises from glandular epithelial tissue (such as mammary ducts and lobules). In modern oncologic surgery, a sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) uses radiotracer or isosulfan blue dye to identify and biopsy the first draining lymph node(s) receiving lymphatic flow from the primary tumor bed. If the sentinel node is negative for malignant cells, the remaining downstream axillary lymph nodes are statistically free of metastasis, sparing the client an extensive complete axillary node dissection and dramatically reducing the lifelong risk of upper extremity lymphedema, nerve damage, and chronic arm pain.

question.stem: The nurse is formulating the preoperative education and clinical care plan for Eleanor. Which nursing interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassure the client that her uterine leiomyoma requires immediate radical total hysterectomy before addressing the breast carcinoma
Instruct the client on postoperative arm care, including avoiding blood draws, intravenous lines, and blood pressure cuffs on the operative right arm if axillary nodes are removed
Inform the client that her urine and skin may exhibit a temporary blue-green discoloration following isosulfan blue dye administration
Assess the client's psychological coping, body image concerns, and connect her with cancer support resources
Encourage vigorous heavy lifting and repetitive upper body weight training immediately within 24 hours postoperatively
Explain that technetium radiotracer and blue dye will be injected around the tumor bed to map the primary lymphatic pathway to the sentinel node

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1430.
question.explanation: Appropriate nursing interventions include: (Option 6) Teaching the physiological basis of sentinel lymph node mapping using radiotracer and blue dye; (Option 3) Preparing the client for harmless transient blue-green discoloration of urine and skin from isosulfan blue; (Option 2) Educating on lymphedema prevention (limb precautions: no venipunctures, injections, or blood pressure measurements on the operative side); and (Option 4) Providing psychosocial support and navigation. The benign uterine leiomyoma is slow-growing and asymptomatic aside from known menorrhagia; the invasive breast carcinoma is an aggressive malignant lesion requiring prioritized surgical and oncologic management. Heavy lifting immediately postoperatively is contraindicated due to risks of wound dehiscence and hematoma.

question.stem: The nurse is preparing Eleanor on the morning of surgery. For each nursing action, click to specify whether the action is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Place a 'Limb Alert' identification band on the right arm and establish peripheral intravenous access exclusively in the left upper extremity
Verify surgical site marking on the right breast performed and confirmed by the operating surgeon with the client awake
Obtain a blood pressure measurement on the right operative arm immediately prior to anesthesia induction
Shave the right axilla and breast with a straight razor 30 minutes prior to surgery
Assess baseline range of motion and sensation in the right shoulder, arm, and digits
Insert a bilateral indwelling nephrostomy tube to monitor intraoperative renal perfusion

question.preamble: Eleanor is admitted to the same-day surgical unit on the day of surgery (0630). The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs from 0630.
question.explanation:
1. Indicated: Placing a limb alert band and utilizing the non-operative left arm for IV access prevents lymphatic trauma and lymphedema.
2. Indicated: Confirming surgical site marking with the client awake is a mandatory Universal Protocol safety step to prevent wrong-site surgery.
3. Contraindicated: Blood pressure cuffs must never be applied to the operative arm due to risk of vascular and lymphatic compromise.
4. Contraindicated: Razor shaving causes microscopic epidermal abrasions that significantly increase surgical site infection risk; if hair removal is needed, surgical clippers are used.
5. Indicated: Establishing baseline neurovascular and range of motion function is critical for detecting postoperative brachial plexus or intercostobrachial nerve injury.
6. Non-Essential: Invasive nephrostomy tubes are completely unnecessary for breast lumpectomy and SLNB.

Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.
question.preamble: Postoperative recovery in the surgical day-stay unit (1400). The nurse has reviewed the Nurses' Notes from 1400 and the Operative & Pathology Summary.
question.explanation:
1. Pathology Evaluation: A finding of pT2N0 (tumor > 2 cm but <= 5 cm, with negative sentinel nodes) confirms that malignant cells have not invaded the regional lymphatic basin, placing the patient in a localized stage with a favorable prognosis and sparing full axillary clearance.
2. Isosulfan Blue Elimination: Green or blue-tinted urine is an expected physiological finding caused by renal excretion of the lymphatic mapping dye.
3. Lymphedema Surveillance: Early symptoms of lymphedema include fullness, heaviness, tightness, and mild edema of the arm. Early detection allows prompt referral for specialized decongestive therapy and compressive garments to prevent permanent fibrotic changes.

Invasive Ductal Carcinoma (Adenocarcinoma). High histologic grade (Grade 3). Markedly anaplastic epithelial cells forming disordered sheets with absence of gland formation. Prominent cellular pleomorphism, frequent atypical mitotic figures, and central areas of coagulative tumor necrosis. High degree of lymphatic channel invasion noted within the stroma. Receptor status: Estrogen Receptor (ER) positive (80%), Progesterone Receptor (PR) positive (65%), HER2/neu negative (IHC 1+).

tabs.title: Surgical Consult Plan
tabs.content: Surgical Proposal: Right lumpectomy with intraoperative sentinel lymph node localization using technetium-99m sulfur colloid radiotracer and intradermal isosulfan blue dye. Frozen section analysis will be performed intraoperatively. If sentinel node is negative, axilla is preserved. If sentinel node shows macrometastatic burden, axillary management will follow standard staging protocol.

tabs.title: Operative & Pathology Summary
tabs.content:
Procedure: Right partial mastectomy (lumpectomy) with sentinel lymph node biopsy × 2.
Pathology: Moderately differentiated invasive ductal adenocarcinoma (Grade 2). Tumor size: 2.8 cm (pT2). Margins: Negative. Sentinel Lymph Nodes: 2 identified (1 blue, 1 hot), both negative for metastatic carcinoma (pN0). Pathologic Stage: Stage IIA (pT2N0M0).
